title: Scale from Zero to Millions
oneLine: Grow a simple application one bottleneck at a time: separate tiers, remove state, cache hot reads, add asynchronous work, replicate, then partition.
opening: I would not begin with microservices or multi-region. I would start with a stateless application and one relational database, instrument it, and evolve only when measurements justify the next step. The normal progression is DNS and CDN at the edge, a load balancer in front of horizontally scaled stateless services, Redis for hot data, a replicated database for read scale and availability, and a queue for slow or bursty work. When the primary database becomes the write bottleneck, I would partition by a stable, high-cardinality key and make the consistency and rebalancing model explicit. At every stage I would call out failure handling, observability, capacity headroom, and what becomes the next bottleneck.
ask: What is the expected DAU, read/write ratio, payload size, and peak-to-average multiplier?
Which operations require strong consistency and which may be eventually consistent?
Is this one region or multi-region, and what are the RTO/RPO expectations?
What is the current bottleneck: CPU, database connections, storage IOPS, network, or a downstream dependency?

functional: Preserve user/session behavior while instances scale

scale: Use a realistic peak multiplier—often 3–10× average rather than designing only for daily average.
Keep 30–50% headroom on critical tiers so an instance or availability zone can fail without immediate overload.
Estimate database connections and IOPS, not only HTTP QPS; they are common first bottlenecks.

decisions.default: Scale vertically briefly, then horizontally behind a load balancer.
decisions.why: Vertical scaling is fast operationally; horizontal scaling removes the single-machine ceiling and improves availability.
decisions.switch: Keep a vertically scaled stateful core when coordination cost dominates or the workload needs very low latency.

decisions.default: Cache-aside for read-heavy objects, with TTL, jitter, and explicit invalidation for critical updates.
decisions.why: It is simple and keeps the database as source of truth while absorbing hot reads.
decisions.switch: Use write-through for simpler read consistency, or event-driven invalidation when stale data is costly.

decisions.default: Read replicas first; partition only when the write set or dataset no longer fits one primary.
decisions.why: Sharding adds cross-shard transactions, rebalancing, hotspot, and operational complexity.
decisions.switch: Partition earlier for tenant isolation, regulatory locality, or an obviously unbounded write workload.

decisions.default: Active-passive or read-local/write-home unless the business truly needs active-active writes.
decisions.why: Single-writer ownership is easier to reason about and avoids conflict resolution on critical entities.
decisions.switch: Use active-active with per-entity home regions, CRDTs, or conflict rules for globally distributed low-latency writes.

deepDives.title: Statelessness
points: Move session state into a shared store or signed token.
Make every instance interchangeable so autoscaling and failover are safe.
Keep idempotency state outside process memory for retried writes.

deepDives.title: Database evolution
points: Separate read and write paths only after measuring replication lag tolerance.
Choose a shard key that is stable, high-cardinality, evenly distributed, and present in common queries.
Plan online resharding using logical ranges, consistent hashing, or a routing directory.

deepDives.title: Degradation
points: Serve cached or partial results when optional dependencies fail.
Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and load shedding.
Protect the database with admission control rather than allowing every upstream retry through.

failures.response: Single-flight requests, TTL jitter, request coalescing, replication of hot values, and a bounded fallback to the database.
Read-your-write routing to primary, version tokens, or route consistency-sensitive reads to the leader.
Detect skew, split logical ranges, isolate celebrity tenants, or add a second-level key while preserving queryability.
Track age-of-oldest-message, autoscale on lag, apply producer backpressure, prioritize classes, and use a DLQ for poison messages.

questions.a: They do not create scale by themselves. They add network calls, distributed failure modes, schema/version coordination, and operational load. Start with clear module boundaries; split a service when ownership, independent scaling, deployment cadence, or fault isolation justify it.

questions.q: How do you make sessions stateless?
questions.a: Use an external session store keyed by an opaque token, or use short-lived signed tokens when the data can be embedded safely. Do not depend on sticky sessions for correctness; they are only an optimization.

questions.q: How would you perform zero-downtime sharding?
questions.a: Introduce a routing layer, dual-write or change-capture during migration, backfill by logical ranges, verify checksums, switch reads per range, then stop old writes. Make every step resumable and observable.

User-facing latency and error rate, saturation, dependency latency, database connections/locks/replication lag, cache hit rate, queue lag, and capacity headroom. Tie alerts to SLO impact rather than raw resource spikes.

mistakes: Listing components without explaining when each becomes necessary
Ignoring database connection limits and downstream amplification
Claiming eventual consistency everywhere without identifying business invariants
seniorSignal: Narrate the design as an evolution driven by evidence. Explicitly state the invariant each component protects, the cost it adds, and how the system behaves during partial failure.
implementation: Spring Boot or ASP.NET stateless APIs behind Kubernetes/Envoy
Redis with TTL jitter and Lua for atomic cache coordination
PostgreSQL primary/read replicas before considering sharding
Kafka for durable asynchronous workflows; OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics, and logs
